newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nomura head resigns over scandal, probe could widen.
newsitem.headline: Nomura head resigns over scandal, probe could widen.

text.p: The head of Japan's leading brokerage resigned Friday over a scandal involving suspected illegal deals and the finance minister said regulators would likely widen a probe of the affair to include other brokerages.

Hideo Sakamaki said he stepped down as president of Nomura Securities Co. Ltd. to atone for the scandal. He becomes an adviser to the company and Chairman Masashi Suzuki takes over his position while retaining the chairmanship.
"As the head of a company which is responsible for what happens in markets, I thought it was important to (resign) from corporate management," Sakamaki told a news conference.

The scandal broke last week when Nomura said two of its directors, who subsequently resigned, had made apparently illegal deals and funnelled funds to a corporate client linked by Japanese media to a former corporate racketeer.
Such racketeers, known as "sokaiya," are often linked to Japan's crime syndicates and typically try to extort money from firms by threatening to expose dubious business practices.
The resignation of Nomura's president, which was no surprise, came amid signs that the scandal may be widening as suspicion fell on other prestigious Japanese brokerages.

Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said Friday that regulators would likely probe Japan's other "Big Four" brokerages after media reports that the corporate client cited in the Nomura scandal also holds accounts at other leading securities houses.
"It's hard to believe the authorities will sit by after such reports. It's common sense for them to conduct an appropriate investigation," Mitsuzuka said.

The Nomura case is another blot on the reputation of corporate Japan after a spate of scandals over unauthorised trading in financial markets, shady oil deals and overly cosy ties in the "iron triangle" of politics, business and bureaucracy.
The scandal also casts a pall over the troubled financial industry's struggle to reform itself to survive increasing competition in the run-up to Japan's "Big Bang" reforms.
Nomura pledged to strive to win back public trust, but the road ahead looks bumpy.
"My first priority is to restore confidence," Suzuki told the news conference. "We will take all possible measures to avoid any repetition of such scandals."

The scandal comes only six years after Sakamaki's predecessor at Nomura stepped down over a similar scandal involving improper compensation of elite clients and links between Nomura affiliates and organised crime.

It latest scandal has already dealt a blow to Nomura's business and reputation, as a number of financial firms, including one in the Nomura group, have suspended dealings with the brokerage pending the outcome of a probe by the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission.
Nomura also faces a possible shareholder suit seeking compensation for any losses resulting from the scandal.

The finance minister could, depending on the SESC findings, revoke Nomura's business licences or order it to halt some or all business for up to six months. Should the deals be found to have violated the commercial code's ban on payoffs to racketeers, legal action could also be initiated.
On the stock market, Nomura shares remained flat at 1,380 yen in heavy-volume trading.

Leading credit rating agency Moody's Investors Service Inc. said Friday that while short-term financial damage to Nomura would likely be limited, the firm faces the challenge of strengthening management control, restoring its reputation and regaining business momentum.
